dervis-irab:1-4.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَحَدٌ): it has been discussed before, and we add to it what Ibn Khālawayh set out, which is a fine passage. He said: "The origin of aḥad is waḥad, i.e. wāḥid, the wāw turning into alif [Translator's note: the source says alif, though the resulting letter is hamza]. There is no wāw in the speech of the Arabs turned into hamza while being fatḥa-vowelled except two words: aḥad, and their saying imraʾa anāt, i.e. sedate (rizān); for the wāw is heavy only with kasra and ḍamma, whereas fatḥa is not heavy, and these two words are anomalous. Ibn Durayd added a third: 'when wealth is purified, its ubla goes', i.e. its wabla." I say: Abū ʿUbayda said he meant its wabla, i.e. its corruption and heaviness, from their saying kalaʾ wabīl, i.e. one that does not agree with the grazing animals. Then he said: "Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim added a fourth: the singular of ālāʾ Allāh is alan, the origin being walā, from awlāhu Allāh maʿrūfan. If you join two wāws, you turn the first into hamza even if it is fatḥa-vowelled, as in your saying in the form fawʿala from waʿada: awʿada, the origin being wawʿada, so they turned the first into hamza, disliking the meeting of two wāws."
(الصَّمَدُ): the one resorted to in needs; it is a faʿal with the sense of mafʿūl, like al-qabḍ meaning al-maqbūḍ. It was also said that al-ṣamad is that which has no hollow interior. In al-Qāmūs: "al-ṣamad with fatḥa on the mīm is the master, because he is resorted to, and the everlasting." The wording of Ibn Khālawayh: "People differed on the explanation of al-ṣamad. The best of what was said is: the master whose mastery has reached its limit and to whom people turn in their needs; he is the goal of people while creatures are in need of His mercy." He recited:
ألا بكر الناعي بخيري بني أسد ... بعمرو بن مسعود وبالسيد الصّمد
(Lo, the announcer came at dawn with news of the best of Banū Asad, ʿAmr ibn Masʿūd and the master, the ṣamad.)
Others said: al-ṣamad is the one who does not eat, and al-ṣamad is that from which nothing comes out:
من كان ذا خوف يخاف من الردى ... فإن خوفي صمد مصمت
(Whoever has fear fears destruction; my fear is a solid, sealed thing.)
And al-ṣamad is the one who remains after the annihilation of His creation." In al-Bukhārī: "Chapter on His saying 'Allah, the Ṣamad'; the Arabs call their nobles al-ṣamad. Abū Wāʾil said: he is the master whose mastery has reached its limit." In al-ʿAynī: he pointed by this to the fact that the meaning of al-ṣamad among the Arabs is nobility, and for this they call their noble chiefs al-ṣamad. From Ibn ʿAbbās: he is the master who has been perfected with all kinds of nobility and mastery; and it was said he is the master resorted to in needs.
(كُفُواً): also kufayʾan on the pattern of faʿīl, and kifāʾ with kasra on the pattern of fiʿāl, with one meaning; al-kufʾ is the like and the peer. Abū Ḥayyān said: it is with ḍamma, kasra and fatḥa on the kāf with sukūn on the fāʾ, and with ḍamma on the kāf and ḍamma on the fāʾ. Ḥamza and Ḥafṣ read it with ḍamma on the kāf; Ḥamza read hamza, while Ḥafṣ replaced it with wāw; the rest of the seven read it with ḍamma and hamza. al-Aʿraj, Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba and Nāfiʿ eased the hamza; and in a report from Nāfiʿ it is kifāʾ, with kasra on the kāf, fatḥa on the fāʾ and a lengthening.

* I'rab:
(قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ) قل is an imperative verb, its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you, O Muḥammad"; and هو has two aspects: 1- that it is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), because it is a place of glorification, as though it were said "the matter is this", namely that Allah is one with no second; the clause after it is a khabar explaining it; 2- that it is a pronoun returning to what is understood from the context, because it is reported among the reasons for its revelation that they said "Describe your Lord to us and trace His lineage", and it was said that they said to him "Is He of copper or of iron?", so it was sent down. In that case, الله may be a mubtadaʾ and أحد its khabar, the clause being the khabar of the first; and أحد may be the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "He is One". The wording of al-Zamakhsharī: "هو is the pronoun of the matter, as in your saying 'He is Zayd, departing', as though it were said: the matter is this, namely that Allah is One with no second. If you say: what is the position of هو? I say: nominative as mubtadaʾ, and the khabar is the clause. If you say: the clause that occurs as a khabar must have a link back to the mubtadaʾ, so where is the link? I say: the ruling of this clause is the ruling of the single term in your saying 'Zayd is your servant', in that it is the mubtadaʾ in meaning; for His words 'Allah is One' are the very matter that it designates. It is not like 'Zayd, his father is departing', for there Zayd and the clause indicate two different meanings, so something must connect them." أحد is a badal from His words الله, or on the basis of "هو أحد", or a second khabar. (اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ) mubtadaʾ and khabar. (لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ كُفُواً أَحَدٌ) These three clauses are linked with the wāw, unlike the first three, because His words «Allah is the Ṣamad» confirm and settle what precedes, and likewise conjunction is left out in «He has not begotten» because it emphasises ṣamadiyya: One who is free of need of everything and whom everything else needs cannot be a father or a son. The author of al-Jawhar al-Maknūn alluded to the places of faṣl (disjunction) by saying:
الفصل ترك عطف جملة أتت ... من بعد أخرى عكس وصل قد ثبت
فافصل لدى التوكيد والإبدال ... لنكتة ونيّة السؤال
وعدم التشريك في حكم جرى ... أو اختلاف طلبا وخبرا وفقد جامع ومع إيهام ... عطف سوى المقصود في الكلام
(Faṣl is leaving out conjunction of a clause that comes after another, the opposite of waṣl, which is established. So disjoin in emphasis and badal, for a subtlety and an intended question; and where there is no sharing in a ruling that has passed, or a difference of request and report, or lack of a joining factor, or with the suggestion of a conjunction other than the intended in the speech.)
And there is waṣl (conjunction) between the last three because they were brought for one purpose and one meaning, namely the negation of likeness and relation from Him, the Exalted, in any respect. The author of al-Jawhar al-Maknūn said:
وصل لدى التشريك في الإعراب ... وقصد رفع اللّبس في الجواب
وفي اتفاق مع الاتصال ... في عقل أو في وهم أو خيال
(Conjoin in shared i'rab, and in intending to remove confusion in the answer, and in agreement with connection, in intellect, imagination or fancy.)
لم is a particle of negation, reversal [of the imperfect to past sense] and jussive; يلد is an imperfect verb, jussive through لم; ولم يولد is conjoined to it; ولم is a conjunction; يكن is an imperfect verb jussive through لم; له is a ḥāl or both are attached to كفوا; and كفوا is the fronted khabar of يكن, and أحد its postponed noun. What follows is an enjoyable debate between al-Zamakhsharī and Abū Ḥayyān about the fronting of له. al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: in eloquent Arabic speech the adverbial that is idle (laghw), not 'settled', is placed late and not fronted, and Sībawayh stated this in his book, so what is the matter with its being fronted in the most eloquent and clearest of speech? I say: this speech was brought only to negate equivalence from the Essence of the Creator, glory be to Him, the Exalted; and the point on which this meaning falls and centres is this adverbial, so for that reason it was the most important thing and the one most deserving of fronting." Abū Ḥayyān said: "This clause is not of this chapter, because in His words «and there has not been to Him an equal, anyone» the preposition and its genitive noun is not complete; rather it is incomplete and cannot be the khabar of كان; it is attached to كفوا and fronted before it, so the implied form is 'and no one has been an equal to Him', i.e. His equivalent. So it is in the sense of an object, attached to كفوا, and fronted before كفوا for emphasis, since it contains the pronoun of the Creator, glory be to Him; and the khabar is placed in the middle even though the origin is lateness, because the lateness of the noun is the end-rhyme (fāṣila), so that is good. On the basis of what we have determined, the i'rab of Makkī and others that له is the khabar and كفوا a ḥāl from أحد is invalid, because it is an incomplete adverbial that cannot be a khabar; and al-Zamakhsharī's question and answer are invalid. Sībawayh spoke only about the adverbial that can be a khabar and can be other than a khabar. Sībawayh said: 'You say: mā kāna fīhā aḥad khayr minka, and mā kāna aḥad mithlaka fīhā, and laysa fīhā aḥad khayr minka when you make فيها settled and do not make it on the basis of "Zayd is standing", you let the adjective follow the noun; but if you make it on the basis of "In it Zayd stands", you put it in the accusative. So you say mā kāna fīhā aḥad khayran minka and mā kāna aḥad khayran minka fīhā; except that when you intend idleness, the later you place the idle one the better, and when you intend it to be settled, the earlier you place it the better. Fronting and delaying, idleness and settledness are all good, abundant Arabic. Allah the Exalted said «and there has not been to Him an equal, anyone», and the poet said: "as long as among them there is a young camel alive".' End of quotation." What we have transferred in summary is in Sībawayh's words, so you see his statement and his illustration with the adverbial that can be a khabar; and the meaning of his "settled" is a khabar of the mubtadaʾ and of كان. If you say: he did give the noble verse as an example, I say: this is what led Makkī, al-Zamakhsharī and others into what they fell into; Sībawayh meant only that the complete adverbial, which is in his words "as long as among them there is a young camel alive", is treated as an extra and not a khabar, just as له in the verse is treated as an extra; so he made the adverbial that could be a khabar like the incomplete adverbial in not being used as a khabar. No one with a sound mind doubts that nothing is established from His words «ولم يكن له أحد»; even if كفوا were delayed and put in the nominative as an adjective, with له made the khabar, no speech would be established from it; rather you see that the negation falls only on the khabar, which is كفوا, and له is attached to it, and the meaning is 'and no one has been His equal'." Ibn al-Munayyir has given on this occasion a subtle point from Sībawayh showing this man's brilliance and sharpness of mind. He said: "It is reported of Sībawayh that he heard one of the coarse Arabs reciting «ولم يكن أحد كفوا له», and this boor followed his habit, his nature being coarse to the subtlety of the meaning for which the adverbial and the khabar are required to be fronted before the noun. For the purpose for which the verse was brought is the negation of equivalence and equality from the Essence of Allah the Exalted, so fronting the equivalence that is meant to be negated from Him was more fitting; then, when it was fronted to be negated, the adverbial was mentioned with it, to show the sanctified Essence by negating equivalence."

* Rhetoric:
The most prominent distinguishing feature of Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ is concision (ījāz); examples of it have preceded, and we shall now try to clarify the purposes latent in its concision, the compactness of its text and the nearness of its two ends, and we shall try to expand on this in a way that makes the intent clear and by which the sought aim is grasped:
1- This surah comprises two of the names of Allah the Exalted that contain all the attributes of perfection, namely al-Aḥad and al-Ṣamad, because they indicate the oneness of the sanctified Essence described with all attributes of perfection. The explanation is that al-Aḥad conveys His particular existence in which no other shares, and al-Ṣamad conveys all attributes of perfection, because He is the one to whom mastery reaches its limit, so the return of all requests is from Him and to Him; and this is not complete in truth except for one who has gathered all the attributes of perfection, and that is fitting only for Allah the Exalted.
2- It includes the direction of belief and sincerity of knowledge, and what must be affirmed for Allah of oneness, which negates any partnership, and ṣamadiyya, which affirms for Him all the attributes of perfection that no deficiency can touch.
3- The negation of child and parent, which settles the perfection of the meaning.
4- The negation of the equal, which contains the negation of the like and peer.
5- They said: Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ is a third of the Qur'an, because the Qur'an is report and composition (inshāʾ), composition being command, prohibition and permission, and report being report about the Creator and report about His creation; and Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ purified the report about Allah and freed its reciter from doctrinal polytheism.
6- Its names are many, and an increase of names indicates the nobility of the named; here is a table of its twenty names with a brief explanation of each name:
1- al-Ikhlāṣ (Sincerity): its meaning has preceded, that it purified the report about Allah and freed its reciter from polytheism.
2- al-Tanzīl: because it fulfilled the most complete purposes by its revelation.
3- al-Tajrīd: because it strips its reciter of polytheism and its motives, and whoever clings to it is stripped of partisanship.
4- al-Tawḥīd: for its containing the attributes of Allah the Exalted, His justice and His oneness. The science of tawḥīd is of the highest rank from Allah, and how could it not be, since knowledge follows the object known, ennobled by its nobility and lowered by its lowness, and the object of this science is Allah the Exalted, His attributes, and what is permissible and impermissible for Him; consider the nobility of its station, the majesty of its place, its excelling over every science and its taking the prize of precedence.
5- al-Najāt (Deliverance): because it delivers its reciter from the Fire.
6- al-Wilāya (Guardianship): because Allah grants guardianship to whoever clings to it.
7- al-Jamāl (Beauty): for its pointing to the beauty of Allah the Exalted, i.e. His being described with perfections and declared free of deficiencies.
8- al-Maʿrifa (Knowledge): because whoever understands it and plumbs its depths knows Allah the Exalted with true knowledge.
9- al-Muqashqisha: from qashqashahu min al-jarab or al-judarī, i.e. he cured him and he was cured; it was so named because it cures its reciter of blemishes and of all motives of polytheism and hypocrisy.
10- al-Muʿawwidha: because it fortifies its reciter against the trials of this world and the next.
11- al-Ṣamad: its discussion has preceded at length.
12- al-Nisba (Lineage): because of the polytheists' saying "Trace your Lord's lineage for us".
13- al-Asās (Foundation): because it is the root of the religion and its pillar.
14- al-Māniʿa (Preventer): because it prevents the trial of the grave and the punishment of the Fire.
15- al-Muḥtaḍir: because the angels attend to listen to it.
16- al-Munaffira: because the devils flee at its recitation.
17- al-Barāʾa (Absolution): because it is an absolution from polytheism.
18- al-Mudhakkira: because it reminds the servant of pure orientation.
19- al-Nūr (Light): because it illuminates the heart.
20- al-Insān: because the human being cannot do without it.
